name: Commercial Electrical Service
shortDescription: Service, repair, and maintenance for commercial properties. Retail, office, restaurant, medical, and warehouse, with off-hours scheduling.

children.text: Commercial Electrical Service in the Phoenix Valley

When something electrical fails at a business, the cost is not the repair. It is the register that will not open, the walk-in that is warming up, the tenant calling property management, and the crew standing around waiting. At
The Wire Guy Electric

, we handle service and maintenance for commercial properties across the Valley: retail centers, offices, restaurants, medical suites, salons, warehouses, and the property managers who look after all of them.
What We Get Called For
Power is out in part of the building.
Tracing a dead circuit back through the panel, the feeder, or a failed device.
Breakers tripping repeatedly.
Usually a load problem, a failing breaker, or equipment that has started drawing more than it should.
Panel and breaker work.
Replacements, additions, and cleanup of panels that have been added to for twenty years without a plan.
New equipment circuits.
A tenant brings in a new oven, compressor, autoclave, or server rack and the existing circuit will not carry it.
Lighting maintenance.
Ballasts, drivers, retrofits, and fixtures across a whole property in one visit rather than one at a time.
Exterior and parking lot lighting.
Pole lights, wall packs, photocells, and timers, which matter for both safety and liability.
Exit and emergency lighting.
Testing, battery replacement, and bringing a building back into shape before an inspection.
Outlets, switches, and devices.
The unglamorous list that keeps a space usable.
Service Calls and Response
We keep commercial service work scheduled so businesses are not waiting a week for somebody to look at a dead circuit. For anything that stops operations, we prioritize accordingly.

We also work after hours when the work requires it. Killing power to a shared panel during business hours is rarely the right answer in an occupied center, and for retail and restaurants it is usually not an option at all. If the job needs a Sunday morning or a 6 a.m. start, that is a scheduling question rather than a problem.
For Property Managers and Multi-Site Operators

If you manage several properties, the thing that saves you time is not the hourly rate. It is having one electrician who already knows where the panels are, which suites share distribution, and what was done last time.

We are set up for that: consistent crews, documentation of what we did and where, and a single point of contact rather than a dispatch queue. For recurring needs like lighting sweeps, exit and emergency testing, and seasonal exterior lighting checks, we would rather schedule the work ahead than react to it.
Preventive Work That Is Actually Worth Doing
Most commercial electrical failures announce themselves. The ones we find on a walkthrough, before they take anything down:
Hot spots and loose connections at panels and disconnects, which are the leading cause of the failures nobody sees coming
Panels that are full, mislabeled, or holding breakers that do not belong in them
Corrosion on exterior equipment, especially after monsoon season
Exit and emergency fixtures with dead batteries, which is the item most likely to fail an inspection
Extension cords and power strips doing the job a dedicated circuit should be doing

name: New Construction Wiring
shortDescription: Full electrical for custom homes, casitas, shops, and additions. Temp power, slab rough, service sizing, complete rough-in and trim out.

children.text: New Construction and Custom Home Wiring in the Phoenix Valley

Wiring a house from bare studs is the one chance anybody gets to do it right without tearing anything open. Every decision made at rough-in either serves the homeowner for thirty years or becomes an expensive retrofit later. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, we wire custom homes, casitas, guest houses, detached shops, and additions across the Valley, working from plans with builders and directly with homeowners building their own.
What a Full New Construction Package Includes
Temporary power.
The construction pole and service so the rest of the trades can work.
Underground and slab rough.
Conduit and sleeves placed before the pour, because everything not sleeved becomes a saw-cut later.
Service and panel.
Sized off a real load calculation for the finished house, not a builder default.
Full rough-in.
Boxes, home runs, circuits, and can layout set before insulation and drywall.
Structured and low voltage.
Data, coax, speaker, camera, and doorbell pathways run while walls are open.
Trim out.
Devices, fixtures, fans, switches, and panel labeling.
Final walkthrough.
Every circuit tested and labeled, with the homeowner walked through their own panel.
Size the Service for the House You Will Actually Live In
This is where we push hardest, because it is the decision most likely to be regretted.

A new Valley home is not the load profile of a 1995 home. Between two AC systems, a pool, a spa, one or two EV chargers, a casita, a shop, and eventually a battery, the connected load adds up fast. A 200-amp service is the baseline we build around for most custom homes, and we run the calculation against what the house will look like in ten years rather than move-in day.

The relevant number for comparison: adding capacity later, once the drywall is up and the meter is set, means a panel or full service replacement that generally runs $5,200 to $6,500 for a standard 200-amp like-for-like, or $6,400 to $8,750 for a full service replacement with a new all-in-one meter base and panel. Doing it correctly during construction costs a fraction of that. Our
panel replacement page
covers what that work involves when it does have to happen after the fact.
Rough-In Is Your Last Cheap Change Order

We walk the house with the homeowner at rough-in, before insulation, and it is the most valuable hour of the project. Standing in the framed space, people see things the plan never showed them: the switch on the wrong side of the door, the outlet the future desk needs, the pendant spacing over an island that is wider than it looked on paper, the missing floor outlet in a great room with no walls near the seating.
Moving a box at that stage takes minutes. Moving it in April after the walls are painted is a drywall repair, a texture match, and a paint call.
Things We Plan For in Arizona Specifically
Attic heat.
A Valley attic runs brutally hot for months. Conductor sizing accounts for ambient derating rather than a chart pulled from a milder climate.
Block and stucco.
Exterior runs get planned before the block goes up, not chased into it afterward.
Casitas, shops, and detached garages.
Feeders and subpanels sized for what actually goes in them, including a mini-split and a compressor rather than a light and a receptacle.
Pool and spa equipment.
Bonding, disconnects, and circuits planned with the pool contractor instead of after they show up.
EV ready.
Even for people who do not own an EV yet, a conduit and a panel space during construction costs almost nothing. See our
EV charger installation page
Solar and battery ready.
Panel space and location planned so a future install does not require moving equipment.
Lighting Is Worth Doing Deliberately

Most new homes get a generic can layout on a grid. The houses that look genuinely finished got a lighting plan: layered ambient, task, and accent, dimmers where they matter, and cabinet and cove lighting built in rather than added later. That is work we specialize in, and rough-in is the only time it is easy. Details on our
custom lighting page

We bid from plans and hold the number.
We hit rough-in dates.
Framing, insulation, and drywall are all stacked behind us and we know it.
Clean work that inspects well.
Straight runs, proper support, correct torque, labeled panel.
We talk to homeowners like adults.
If a request is a bad idea, you hear why, along with a better option.

children.text: Tenant Improvement Electrical in the Phoenix Valley
A tenant improvement job lives and dies on schedule. The lease is signed, the rent clock is running, and every trade in the space is waiting on somebody else to finish. At
The Wire Guy Electric

, we do TI electrical for general contractors, property managers, and business owners across Mesa, Gilbert, Chandler, Tempe, Scottsdale, and Queen Creek. We build from your plans, we show up when we said we would, and we do not hold up the drywall crew.
What We Handle on a TI Build
Shell and whitebox buildouts.
Taking a bare space to a finished, occupiable suite: service and panel, feeders, branch circuits, lighting, and devices.
Demo and rework.
Removing what the last tenant left behind, tracing abandoned circuits, and cleaning up the ceiling grid so the new layout starts from a known state.
Panels and subpanels.
Sizing the distribution for the actual connected load of the new use, not the last one. A salon suite and a dental office in the same shell have very different demands.
Lighting layouts and controls.
Troffers, cans, linear, and track, plus the occupancy sensing and daylight controls that commercial energy code expects.
Dedicated equipment circuits.
Ovens, compressors, autoclaves, dryers, POS, server closets, and whatever the tenant is bringing that nobody mentioned until week three.
Emergency and exit lighting.
Sized and placed for egress. More on that on our
emergency and exit lights page
Low voltage rough-in coordination.
Pathways and boxes for data, security, and AV so the other vendors are not cutting into finished walls later.
The Space Types We See Most

Retail suites in strip centers. Office and flex space. Medical and dental. Salon and barber suites. Restaurants and quick-serve, which are their own category of electrical work because of the equipment schedule and the hood. Warehouse and light industrial. Gyms and studios.

Each one has a different load profile and a different set of things that go wrong when the electrical was bid off a generic square-foot number rather than the actual equipment list. We ask for the equipment schedule early, because that is the document that determines whether the existing service is adequate.
How We Work with General Contractors

Most of our TI work comes through GCs, and the ones we work with repeatedly tell us the same things matter: hit the rough-in date, be ready for inspection when you say you are, and communicate the moment something in the field does not match the plan.

That last one is the real value. Existing conditions in a twenty-year-old retail bay are rarely what the as-builts show. When we open a wall and find the panel feeding the neighboring suite, or a ceiling full of circuits nobody can account for, you hear about it that day with a proposed solution and a cost, not at the end of the job as a change order surprise.
We also work after hours and around occupied neighbors when the center is live. Shutting down a shared panel at 2 p.m. on a Saturday is how you make enemies of every other tenant in the building.
Working Around an Occupied Building

Plenty of TI work happens in centers and office buildings that never close. We phase shutdowns, coordinate with property management on notice to neighboring tenants, and schedule anything that interrupts shared distribution for off-hours. If the space is being turned over while the business next door is running, that constraint belongs in the plan from day one, not discovered mid-project.
Why Contractors Call Us Back
We bid from plans and hold the number.
If the scope changes, we tell you before we do the work.
Field problems come with solutions.
Existing conditions in an older Valley building are always a surprise. What matters is how fast you get an answer.
Inspection-ready work.
Grounding, bonding, clearances, and labeling done to code the first time so nothing gets red-tagged and rescheduled.
We coordinate with the other trades.
Mechanical, plumbing, low voltage, and fire all want the same ceiling. We sort that out on site rather than in a punch list.

children.text: Exterior Electrical in the Phoenix Valley

Outdoor electrical in Arizona is a different job than outdoor electrical anywhere else. Everything you install lives in direct sun at 115 degrees, gets sandblasted by haboob dust, then takes sideways rain for two months of monsoon. Equipment that would last twenty years in a mild climate gives up here in five. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, we build exterior work to survive that, not just to pass a first look.
What We Install Outside
Exterior outlets and GFCI receptacles
in weatherproof in-use covers, which is the only kind that actually protects a cord that stays plugged in.
Landscape and path lighting
, including transformer sizing and burial depth done properly so the run does not fail at the first splice.
Security and flood lighting
, motion sensing, dusk-to-dawn photocells, and camera power.
Patio, pergola, and ramada power
for fans, heaters, TVs, and misting systems.
Detached structures.
Feeders and subpanels for garages, shops, casitas, and sheds.
Pool and spa equipment circuits
, including bonding and disconnects.
Gate, well, and irrigation controller power.
EV charger circuits
routed on exterior walls. More on our
EV charger installation page
Why Outdoor Work Fails Here
Almost every exterior repair we get called for traces back to one of four things.
UV.
Standard PVC and non-rated cable go chalky and brittle in Arizona sun. We use UV-rated conduit and fittings on anything exposed, because the sun finds everything else.
Water intrusion.
A cover that is weatherproof only when closed does nothing for the cord you leave plugged in year-round. In-use covers and correct fitting orientation are what keep water out of a box.
Bad splices underground.
Landscape lighting is where we find the worst of it: wire nuts buried in dirt, no direct-burial connectors, no protection at all. Those work for one season.
Undersized runs.
Long runs to a back-yard structure lose voltage. Lights dim, motors run hot, equipment wears out early. That is a wire-sizing decision, made once, at install.
Landscape Lighting Worth Paying For

Good landscape lighting is a design job as much as an electrical one: light the trees and the architecture, hide the fixtures, and avoid the runway-of-path-lights look. We plan the layout with you, size the transformer with headroom for expansion, and use direct-burial rated connections throughout. Cost detail is in our
landscape lighting cost guide
Why Homeowners Choose Us for Exterior Work
Built for this climate.
UV-rated materials, in-use covers, proper burial, correct wire sizing.
Clean routing.
Conduit run straight and tight to the wall, not draped across stucco.
We plan for what is next.
Extra capacity so adding a fan or a charger later is not a new project.

children.text: Light Fixture Replacement in the Phoenix Valley
Swapping a light fixture looks like a fifteen-minute job until you get the old one down and find out what is behind it. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, fixture replacement is one of our most common calls, and a good share of them turn into a conversation about the box, the wiring, or the switch rather than the fixture itself.
What We Replace
Ceiling fixtures and flush mounts
throughout the house
Chandeliers
in entries, dining rooms, and stairwells, which usually need a rated box and real bracing
Pendants
over islands and nooks, hung level and spaced correctly
Vanity and bath fixtures
, including wet-rated units over tubs and showers
Ceiling fans
, which need a fan-rated box every time, not the box that was already there
Exterior fixtures
, sconces, and flood lights
Old fluorescent kitchen boxes
swapped for recessed cans or modern flush mounts
What We Find When the Old Fixture Comes Down
This is the part worth knowing before you buy a fixture.
The box is not rated for the weight.
A heavy chandelier or a fan on a standard plastic box is a real failure risk. Fans especially, because vibration works fasteners loose over years.
The wiring is brittle.
In older Valley homes, decades of heat in an attic makes conductor insulation crack right at the box, exactly where it gets flexed during a swap.
There is no ground.
Older two-wire circuits are common in homes wired before grounding was standard, and it changes what can safely be installed.
The dimmer does not match the fixture.
The most frequent complaint we hear after a DIY swap is buzzing or flickering LEDs. That is almost always an old dimmer designed for incandescent load trying to run an LED driver.
Bringing Your Own Fixture

Most people do, and that is fine. Two things help: have it on site before we arrive, and open the box to check the parts are all there. If you want a second opinion on whether something will look right in the space or work with your ceiling, ask before you buy. We would rather tell you up front than after it is hanging.
When a Swap Is Not the Right Answer

Sometimes the fixture is not the problem. If a room is dim because it has one central light and no other sources, a better fixture will not fix that. Recessed cans, or a layered plan with task and accent light, is the actual answer. Details on our

shortDescription: Custom cabinet lighting cut and soldered to fit, plus recessed cans, chandeliers, pendants, and cove runs. Hardwired and seamless.

children.text: Custom Lighting in the Phoenix Valley
Most electricians will install whatever fixture you hand them. That's fine for a basic swap, but it's not what we do best. At
The Wire Guy Electric

, custom lighting is where we get to be craftsmen. Recessed cans cut exactly where they need to be. Chandeliers hung properly with the right box and bracing. Pendants balanced and level. And our specialty: custom cabinet lighting, cut and soldered to fit each cabinet run, hardwired, and completely seamless.
Custom Cabinet Lighting (Our Specialty)

This is what separates a real install from a hardware-store kit. Most under-cabinet lighting on the market comes in pre-cut, fixed lengths: 12", 18", 24", 36". They don't fit your cabinets. They leave dark gaps, or they hang over the edges, or they get cut down with plastic end caps that look cheap.
We do it differently. For each cabinet, we measure the exact interior length and
cut and solder a continuous LED strip to fit
. Every joint is soldered and sealed, not crimped. Every run is
hardwired back to a dedicated switch or dimmer

, not plugged into an outlet with a dangling cord. The driver is tucked into the cabinet or adjacent wall so nothing is visible. The result is a single, seamless line of light that runs the full length of each cabinet with no gaps, no visible wiring, and no bulky joints.
Done right, you don't see the lights. You see what they light up.
Continuous strip, custom-cut and soldered
for each cabinet length
Hardwired
to a dedicated switch or dimmer (no plug-in drivers)
Seamless installation
with hidden wiring and driver placement
Color temperature
matched to your kitchen (warm white, natural, or tunable)
Dimmable
on most installs, controlled from the wall or through smart home systems
Recessed Can Lighting

Recessed cans are still the single most popular lighting upgrade our customers ask for. We do them right: properly spaced for even coverage, IC-rated where they touch insulation, wet-rated in bathrooms and soffits, and wired on dimmers where it makes sense. New construction retrofits, ceiling cut-ins for existing homes, and full-house lighting plans. Full pricing detail:

Chandeliers

A chandelier is usually heavier than a standard fixture, and a lot of older Phoenix homes don't have the right box or bracing to support one. We install an approved fan-rated or heavy-fixture ceiling box, add bracing in the attic or ceiling cavity, run new wire if the existing is undersized, and hang the fixture level and centered. Dining rooms, foyers, stairwells, and great rooms.
Pendant Lighting

Kitchen islands, breakfast nooks, hallways, and bathrooms. Proper spacing, consistent drop heights, straight and level alignment, dimmer-compatible wiring. We can work from your design, your designer's plan, or help you figure out what will actually look right in the space.

children.text: Commercial LED Lighting and Retrofits in the Phoenix Valley
Lighting is usually the largest electrical line on a commercial utility bill, and in most Valley buildings it is also the oldest system in the place. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, we handle LED conversions and new installs for retail, office, warehouse, and industrial spaces across the Valley.
What We Do
Full LED retrofits.
Converting existing fluorescent or HID lighting over to LED, either by replacing fixtures outright or retrofitting the existing housings.
New installs.
Layout and installation for new spaces, buildouts, and expansions.
High bay and warehouse.
Replacing metal halide and high-output fluorescent with LED high bays, which is usually the single biggest efficiency win in an industrial space.
Troffers and office lighting
in drop ceilings.
Exterior, parking lot, and wall packs
, including photocell and timer control.
Lighting controls.
Occupancy sensing, daylight harvesting, and zoning, which commercial energy code increasingly expects.
Why LED Actually Pays Off Here

The energy savings are real, but in Arizona there is a second effect people forget: the lighting you remove was also a heat source. Older fluorescent and metal halide fixtures dump meaningful heat into a conditioned space, and your AC pays to remove it. In a Valley summer that is not a rounding error.

The third saving is labor. Replacing lamps and ballasts across a large space is an ongoing cost that mostly disappears with LED, and in high-ceiling spaces where every replacement means a lift, that alone can justify the project.
Doing the Retrofit Without Closing

Most of these jobs happen in occupied buildings. We phase the work by area, schedule anything disruptive for off-hours, and keep the space usable while the conversion is underway. For retail and restaurants that usually means early mornings or after close, which is a scheduling question rather than a problem.
Getting the Specification Right
Color temperature
chosen for the use, not for whatever was on the shelf. Retail and hospitality generally want warmer light than a warehouse.
Consistency.
Mismatched color across a space is the most common complaint after a partial retrofit done piecemeal.
Output matched to the task
, since more lumens is not automatically better and glare is a real problem in offices.
Driver quality.
The driver is what fails first on a cheap fixture. In a high-ceiling space, a cheap driver is an expensive lift call later.

Every business eventually outgrows the outlets it was built with. New equipment arrives, the layout changes, somebody adds a workstation, and suddenly there is a power strip chain running along a baseboard. At

for equipment that should not share, covered further on our

The Power Strip Problem

Almost every commercial space we walk into has at least one. A power strip feeding another power strip, an extension cord run under a rug, or a printer and a space heater sharing a fifteen-amp circuit with six workstations.

It is worth taking seriously, because it is both a fire risk and a code problem that shows up on inspections. It is also usually cheap to fix. Adding the receptacle where the equipment actually lives is generally a small job compared to the risk it removes.
Repairs and Replacements

Commercial devices see far more cycles than residential ones. Switches wear out, receptacles lose grip and stop holding a plug, and connections loosen. A receptacle that no longer grips is not just annoying, it is a heat problem at the contact.
We also replace devices that are simply old: worn, discolored, painted over, or damaged. In customer-facing spaces this is a surprisingly visible detail.

children.text: Storefront and Sign Lighting in the Phoenix Valley
A dark storefront reads as closed, even at 7 p.m. on a Tuesday when you are very much open. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, we install and repair storefront, sign, and facade lighting for businesses across the Valley.
What We Handle
Sign lighting and power
, including circuits for illuminated and channel-letter signs
Facade and building lighting
, wall washing and accent lighting on the building itself
Entry and canopy lighting
, which drives both visibility and safety
Awning and soffit lighting
Window and display lighting
for retail
Photocells and timers
so the lighting runs on a schedule rather than on somebody remembering
Parking and walkway lighting
, covered further on our
commercial service page
What Arizona Does to Storefront Lighting
Everything on the front of your building faces the worst conditions in the Valley: full sun most of the day, dust driven into every housing, and sideways rain through monsoon season.

That means UV-rated materials on anything exposed, in-use covers where cords stay connected, correct gasketing on fixtures, and drivers rated for the ambient temperature they will actually see. A driver spec'd for a mild climate installed behind a west-facing sign is a service call waiting to happen.
Dust is the underrated one. It accumulates on lenses and cuts output significantly over a couple of seasons, which is why a sign that looks dim is often not failing at all, just filthy.
Repairs and Maintenance

Most of our storefront calls are half-lit signs, dead sections, photocells stuck on or off, and fixtures taken out by a storm. When a section goes dark it is usually a driver, a photocell, or a connection that let water in, and it is worth fixing quickly since a partially lit sign looks worse than one that is off entirely.

Support that is actually rated.

Commercial fixtures get heavy, and a decorative fixture over a dining area is not a place to find out the box was not rated for it. We install proper support and bracing, and in a drop ceiling that means tying into structure above rather than the grid.
Height and spacing.
Too low over a bar and people hit them. Too high and the fixture stops doing its job. Spacing has to relate to the furniture below, which means it should be set after the layout is known.

Working With Your Designer

Plenty of these projects come with a designer or architect already specifying fixtures. That works well, and the earlier we see the spec the better. name: Commercial Electrical Troubleshooting
shortDescription: Dead circuits, repeat trips, voltage problems, overheating terminations, and the intermittent faults nobody else can pin down.

children.text: Commercial Electrical Troubleshooting in the Phoenix Valley
When a circuit goes down in a business, the clock starts immediately. Product is warming, the line is stopped, the register is dead, or a suite full of people has nothing to do. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, we diagnose commercial electrical faults across the Valley and fix the cause rather than the symptom.
What We Diagnose
Dead circuits and partial outages
where the breaker never tripped
Breakers that trip repeatedly
, especially under load or at the same time each day
Equipment that keeps failing
, which is often a supply problem rather than an equipment problem
Voltage problems
, including drops under load and imbalance across phases
Overheating
at panels, disconnects, and terminations
Lighting that flickers or drops out
in sections
Nuisance GFCI tripping
Intermittent faults
, the ones that never happen while anybody is looking
How We Approach It

Commercial systems are harder to trace than residential ones because there is more of everything: more distribution, more panels, more circuits that were added over the years by people who did not label anything.

So the first job is usually understanding what is actually there. We map the distribution, identify what is on the affected circuit, and test methodically from the load back toward the source. Thermal inspection is useful here, because heat shows up at a failing connection well before it fails outright.

The common causes are consistent: loose or corroded terminations, a failing breaker, an undersized circuit that has quietly been overloaded since somebody added equipment, a damaged conductor, or a neutral problem on a shared circuit.
Intermittent Problems

These are the frustrating ones, and they are also the ones most worth solving properly. A fault that appears only under load, or only in the afternoon heat, is telling you something specific: something is marginal and temperature or current is pushing it over the line.
Those almost always get worse. Finding them while they are intermittent is considerably cheaper than finding them after they take equipment or a full circuit down.
What Should Not Wait
Any burning smell near a panel, disconnect, or piece of equipment
A panel or disconnect that is warm, buzzing, or discolored
Scorch marks at any termination
Repeated breaker trips on a circuit serving critical equipment
Any shock reported by staff

children.text: Emergency and Exit Lighting in the Phoenix Valley

Exit and emergency lighting is the system nobody thinks about until an inspection or an actual emergency, and it is also the system most likely to be quietly non-functional. The fixture on the wall looks fine. The battery inside it died two years ago. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, we install, test, and repair egress lighting for commercial properties across the Valley.
What We Handle
Exit sign installation
and placement along egress paths
Emergency lighting
, both the classic twin-head units and integrated fixtures with battery backup
Battery replacement

Testing
and correcting whatever fails it
Replacing dead or damaged units
Retrofits

Adding coverage
where a layout change left a path unlit
Why These Fail Quietly

The fixture is powered and the indicator light is on, so everything appears fine. But the indicator only tells you the unit is receiving power. It does not tell you the battery still holds a charge, which is the only thing that matters when the power goes out.

Batteries have a finite service life, and Arizona heat shortens it. A unit mounted in a warehouse, a stairwell, or anywhere near a roof deck sees ambient temperatures that age a battery considerably faster than the spec sheet assumes.

This is why the only real test is the actual test: kill power to the unit and confirm it illuminates for the required duration. That is a straightforward thing to do on a schedule and the single best way to avoid finding out during an inspection.
Layout Changes Create Gaps

Something we find often: a building's egress lighting was correct when it was installed, then a tenant improvement moved walls, added a corridor, or changed the exit path. The lighting stayed where it was.
Any time a space gets reconfigured, the egress path and its lighting should be reviewed against the new layout. If you are planning a buildout, that belongs in scope from the start. See our

name: Dedicated Circuits
shortDescription: Dedicated circuits for commercial equipment. Kitchen, refrigeration, medical, salon, and server loads sized off the nameplate.

children.text: Dedicated Circuits for Commercial Equipment in the Phoenix Valley

A dedicated circuit serves one piece of equipment and nothing else. It sounds like a small distinction. In practice it is the difference between equipment that runs reliably for years and equipment that keeps tripping, keeps failing, and keeps costing you service calls. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, we design and install dedicated circuits for commercial equipment across the Valley.
When Equipment Needs Its Own Circuit
Anything with a compressor or a motor.
Refrigeration, walk-ins, air compressors, and HVAC draw a large surge at startup that drags voltage down for everything sharing the circuit.
Commercial kitchen equipment.
Ovens, fryers, warmers, dishwashers, and ice machines.
Medical and dental equipment
, including autoclaves and imaging.
Salon equipment
, dryers and processors that pull hard and continuously.
Server racks, network gear, and point of sale.
These are sensitive to what everything else on the circuit is doing.
Shop machinery and anything with a duty cycle.
What Sharing Actually Costs You
Two things go wrong when equipment shares a circuit it should not.

The first is nuisance tripping. Total draw exceeds the breaker when two things happen to run at once, usually at the worst possible time, and staff learn to reset the breaker as a routine rather than report it.

The second is quieter and more expensive. Motor startups cause voltage dips, and sensitive electronics on the same circuit see those dips. That shows up as equipment that reboots, corrupts data, or simply fails early for no visible reason. Nobody connects it back to the compressor cycling in the back room, but that is often exactly what is happening.
How We Size It

Off the equipment nameplate, every time. The nameplate gives the minimum circuit ampacity and the maximum overcurrent protection, and that is what the conductor and breaker get sized to, not a rule of thumb.

Continuous loads need additional headroom. Long runs need conductor sizing that accounts for voltage drop, which matters more than people expect in a warehouse. And in Arizona, ambient temperature derating is real: a conductor run through an uninsulated roof space is not operating at the temperature the base table assumes.

Signs the Ballast Is Failing
Tubes that flicker or strobe, especially when first switched on
An audible hum or buzz from the fixture

Discoloration at the tube ends
New tubes that fail quickly, which usually means the ballast, not the tubes

Repair or Convert to LED?
This is the real decision, and it is worth thinking about rather than defaulting.
Replacing a ballast makes sense when you have a small number of failures in a fixture set that is otherwise in good shape, or when budget timing means a full conversion has to wait.

Converting to LED usually makes more sense when you are replacing ballasts repeatedly across a space, when the fixtures are old enough that more failures are certain, or when the space has high ceilings where every service call means a lift. In that last case the labor of ongoing maintenance frequently outweighs the cost of converting.

There is also a hard reality worth planning around: fluorescent lamp and ballast availability has been shrinking, and specific tube types get harder to source over time. If your building depends on a type that is being phased down, converting on your schedule beats converting in an emergency. More on our

Most people call us for an inspection at one of three moments: they are buying a house, they are selling one and an inspector flagged something, or something in their current home has started behaving badly enough to worry them. At

Buying a home.

What We Look At
The panel and service.

Brand and age, condition of the bus and lugs, breaker sizing against the conductors they protect, grounding and bonding, available capacity, and whether the panel is on the recall list. Federal Pacific, Zinsco, Challenger, and Pushmatic all get flagged, and we explain why in our post on

The wiring.

What type it is and what condition it is in where we can see it. In homes from the 1960s and 1970s that includes checking for single strand aluminum branch wiring, which is a genuine fire risk at connections and needs proper treatment.
Devices and protection.

GFCI protection where it is required, especially kitchens, baths, garages, and exteriors. Arc-fault protection. Grounded versus ungrounded receptacles, and three-prong outlets that were installed on two-wire circuits with no ground behind them.
The parts nobody looks at.
Attic junctions, exterior disconnects, the meter base, and outdoor equipment that has been baking in the sun since the house was built.

name: Troubleshooting
shortDescription: Dead outlets, repeat breaker trips, flickering lights, buzzing, and burning smells. We map the circuit and find the cause, not the symptom.

children.text: Electrical Troubleshooting in Mesa and the Phoenix Valley

Something is not working and nobody can tell you why. A room went dead. Half the outlets in the kitchen quit. The lights dim every time the AC starts. A breaker trips at the same time every evening and nobody can find the cause. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, troubleshooting is the work we are best at, because it is the work that rewards actually knowing what you are looking at.
What We Get Called For
Part of the house has no power
and the breaker is not tripped
A breaker trips repeatedly
, sometimes on a schedule, sometimes only in the heat
Outlets that quit
, usually a whole run of them at once
Lights that flicker or dim
when large appliances start
Burning smells, warm outlets, or a warm panel
, which is the one to call about today
Buzzing
from a switch, fixture, panel, or disconnect
GFCIs that will not reset
Shocks or tingles
from an appliance or fixture
How We Actually Find It

Most electrical faults are not where the symptom is. A dead bedroom outlet is often caused by a failed connection in a completely different room, because outlets are wired in runs and the break is upstream of what you noticed.

So we map the circuit rather than guess at it. We identify what is actually on the affected circuit, test where power stops, and work back to the fault. That usually lands on one of a short list: a backstabbed device that has loosened over decades, a junction connection cooked by heat, a failing breaker, a damaged conductor, or a shared neutral doing something it should not.
The reason this matters: replacing the outlet you can see does nothing if the problem is a connection two rooms away. That fix appears to work and fails again a month later.
Why Valley Homes Fail in Specific Ways

Arizona heat is hard on connections. Attic temperatures cycle brutally every day for months, conductors expand and contract, and connections that were merely adequate at install work themselves loose. Loose connections generate heat, and heat accelerates the process. That is why so many of our summer calls are intermittent problems that get worse in the afternoon.

Dust and monsoon moisture take care of the exterior side, and homes wired in the 1960s and 1970s can carry single strand aluminum branch wiring, which needs proper treatment at every connection. We cover that in our post on
aluminum wiring in older Phoenix homes

A burning or hot-plastic smell anywhere near a panel, outlet, or fixture
An outlet or switch plate that is warm or discolored
Scorch marks around a receptacle
A panel that buzzes, or that is warm to the touch
Any shock, even a small one, from an appliance or fixture
Those are not wait-and-see items. Our post on

shortDescription: Kitchen, bath, and whole-house remodel electrical. Circuits, GFCI and AFCI protection, layered lighting, and the old wiring behind your walls.

children.text: Kitchen and Bathroom Remodel Electrical in the Phoenix Valley

Kitchens and baths are the two remodels we do most, and they are also the two where the electrical is most likely to be underestimated. Once the cabinets come off the wall and the tile comes up, what is behind them is frequently not what anybody assumed. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, we do remodel electrical for homeowners, designers, and general contractors across Mesa, Scottsdale, Gilbert, Chandler, Tempe, and Queen Creek.
What a Kitchen Actually Needs
A modern kitchen is one of the densest electrical spaces in a house, and older Valley kitchens were not built for it. A typical remodel involves:
Small appliance circuits
serving the countertop receptacles, which in most older kitchens means adding circuits rather than reusing what is there
Dedicated circuits
for the refrigerator, dishwasher, disposal, and microwave
A 240-volt range or cooktop circuit
, sized to the appliance, plus a separate circuit if the wall oven is going somewhere else
GFCI protection
on countertop and island receptacles, and arc-fault protection where required
Island and peninsula power
, which has to be planned with the cabinet maker because there is often only one workable location
Lighting in layers
: recessed for general light, pendants over the island, and under-cabinet for the counters

Under-cabinet lighting is worth doing properly rather than with a hardware store kit. We cut and solder continuous runs to fit each cabinet and hardwire them to a switch or dimmer, so there are no gaps, no visible cords, and no plug-in drivers. Details on our
custom lighting page
What a Bathroom Actually Needs
GFCI protection
on all receptacles, which is the single most common thing missing in older Valley bathrooms
A dedicated circuit
for the receptacles, separate from the lighting
Proper exhaust ventilation
, correctly sized and vented outside rather than into the attic, on a timer or humidity sensor
Vanity lighting
placed to light a face rather than the top of a head, which is a fixture-placement decision made at rough-in
Wet-rated fixtures
in and over showers and tubs
Heated floor and mirror circuits
, if those are in the plan, because both need to be run before tile
The Panel Question

A kitchen remodel usually adds several circuits to a house. If your panel is full, or already carrying an AC system and an EV charger, that is a conversation to have at the start of the project rather than the middle.

Sometimes the answer is a subpanel. Sometimes it is a replacement. For reference, a standard 200-amp like-for-like panel replacement in the Valley generally runs $5,200 to $6,500, and a full service replacement with a new all-in-one meter base and panel is typically $6,400 to $8,750. Not every remodel triggers one. But finding out at demo is much better than finding out the week the cabinets arrive. More on our
panel replacement page
What We Find Behind Old Walls
Open walls are the only time some of this is visible, and remodels are when we catch it:
Single strand aluminum branch wiring
in homes wired in the 1960s and 1970s, which is a genuine fire risk at connections and should be addressed while the walls are open. We wrote about it in detail here:
aluminum wiring in older Phoenix homes
Ungrounded two-wire circuits
feeding outlets that somebody replaced with three-prong receptacles
Junction boxes buried in walls
with no access, which is both a code problem and a reliability problem
Circuits daisy-chained
across rooms in ways that make no sense until you map them
Backstabbed devices
that have been loosening for thirty years
None of this is a reason to panic. All of it is dramatically cheaper to fix while the walls are already open, which is the entire argument for handling it now.
Beyond Kitchens and Baths

We do the rest of it too: whole-house remodels, laundry rooms, garage conversions, casita and guest suite buildouts, home offices that need real circuits, and additions. The approach is the same. Walk it first, plan the circuits against what the space will actually be used for, and rough it in before anything closes up.
How We Quote

Two ways. Send us blueprints or a designer's plan and we will put together a bid from the drawings. Or have us out for a walkthrough, which costs nothing, and we will talk through the scope in the actual space. For most homeowners the walkthrough is more useful, because plans rarely show where the existing circuits are.

children.text: Electrical Panel Replacements in Mesa, Scottsdale, and the Phoenix Valley

Your electrical panel is the heart of your home's electrical system. When it starts to fail, fill up, or fall behind what modern homes demand, everything else downstream suffers: breakers trip, lights flicker, AC compressors short-cycle, and EV chargers can't get enough power to charge overnight. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, panel work is one of the things we do most often. Arizona ROC #365306, fully insured, and coordinated directly with APS or SRP from start to finish.
What We Do
200-amp like-for-like replacement.
The job we do most often. Old 200-amp panel comes out, new Square D, Siemens, or Eaton panel goes in. Same service size, fresh equipment, all new breakers.
Full service replacement (all-in-one meter base and panel).
When the meter base itself is corroded, undersized, or out of spec, we replace the whole assembly as a single combo unit.
Recall-brand replacements.

Old Zinsco, Federal Pacific (FPE), Challenger, and Pushmatic panels are a known fire hazard. If you have one, it needs to come out. We replace with new Square D, Siemens, or Eaton panels rated for today's loads.
Service upgrades (200 to 400 amp).

Adding a pool, hot tub, EV charger, casita, or second AC unit can push your home past what existing service can handle. We do the load calculation, coordinate with SRP or APS for the meter pull, and get you upgraded.
Panel relocations.
Moving a panel from inside a garage to an exterior wall, or shifting it to accommodate a remodel. Includes new meter base, service conductors, grounding system, and utility coordination.
Subpanel installs.
Sometimes the right answer isn't a full main upgrade. Adding a subpanel for a new garage workshop, casita, or EV charger circuit is often faster and cheaper.
Signs You Need a Panel Replacement
Breakers that trip repeatedly, especially when your AC kicks on
A panel brand on the recall list (Zinsco, Federal Pacific, Challenger, Pushmatic)
An aging panel that's 25+ years old with loose lugs, corrosion, or buzzing
No room left for new breakers
Burn marks, rust, or buzzing at the panel
Lights that dim when large appliances turn on
You're planning to add solar, an EV charger, a hot tub, or a casita

name: Recessed Lighting
shortDescription: Recessed can lighting laid out around how you use the room. IC-rated where required, dimmers included, clean retrofit into existing ceilings.

children.text: Recessed Lighting Installation in the Phoenix Valley

Recessed lighting is the single most requested upgrade we do. It takes a room lit by one dim fixture in the middle of the ceiling and makes it feel finished. Done well, you stop noticing the lights and start noticing the room. Done poorly, you get a grid of hot spots and dark corners. At
The Wire Guy Electric
, the difference is in the layout, and the layout is free to get right at the planning stage.
Layout Is the Whole Job
Most bad recessed installs are bad because somebody spaced the cans evenly across a ceiling without thinking about what is under them.

We plan around how the room is used. Cans pulled off the walls far enough to avoid scalloping. Spacing set by ceiling height rather than a fixed number. Light placed over the counters, the seating, and the work surfaces instead of the middle of the walkway. Wall washing where there is art or a feature wall.
In a kitchen this matters most, because standing at your own counter in your own shadow is the most common complaint we hear about a lighting job somebody else did.
Getting the Light Itself Right
Color temperature.

2700K reads warm and residential. 3000K is a clean neutral most people like in kitchens and baths. Above that starts feeling like an office. Consistency across a room matters more than the exact number.
Dimming.
Worth it on almost every install. A kitchen at full output at 9 p.m. is unpleasant, and dimmers cost very little at install time.
Beam spread and trim.
Baffle trims cut glare. Adjustable trims aim light at art or a wall.
IC rating.
Required anywhere a can contacts insulation, which in a Valley attic is most of them.
Wet and damp rating
for showers, soffits, and covered patios.
Retrofit into an Existing Ceiling

You do not need an open ceiling for this. We cut in from below, fish the circuits, and patch as we go. In a single-story home with attic access it is straightforward. Two-story ceilings and vaulted or coffered ceilings take more planning, and second-floor rooms with a floor above rather than an attic are the ones worth walking before quoting.
We are careful about what we cut into. Joists, ducting, and existing runs are all up there, and finding them first is the difference between a clean install and a drywall repair.
What It Costs
The number depends on how many cans, ceiling access, and whether we are adding a circuit or extending an existing one. We break it down in detail in our
recessed lighting installation cost guide
Why Homeowners Choose Us
We plan the layout with you.
On paper, in the room, before anything gets cut.
Clean cuts and clean patches.
Minimal drywall damage, and we know what is above the ceiling before the hole saw comes out.
Consistent color and dimming
across the whole install so no room looks like a different house.

Arizona ROC #365306.

Under the Planning and Development Department’s EV charger guidance, a home charger can be reviewed and permitted over the counter when the existing electrical service is 200 amps single-phase or less and does not need an upgrade; a charger that requires upgrading the service beyond 200 amps single-phase goes to formal plan review.

Phoenix is split between APS and SRP: APS serves much of central and north Phoenix, and SRP serves other parts of the city, including Ahwatukee. For a panel upgrade, SRP’s service specifications say to contact both SRP and the permitting authority first, and SRP reconnects power once both approve the work; APS energizes a new, relocated or replaced meter only after the inspection authority approves the wiring.

title: How Many Circuits Does a Kitchen Need? An Arizona Remodel Wiring Guide
excerpt: A modern kitchen needs seven or eight circuits. Most Valley kitchens built before 2000 have three. Here is what a remodel actually requires and when to wire it.

children.text: Here is the conversation we have in a lot of Valley kitchens. The cabinets are picked, the quartz is ordered, the contractor has a start date. Somebody asks what the electrical is going to run. And the honest answer is that it depends almost entirely on how many circuits are in that kitchen right now, which nobody has looked at yet.

A modern kitchen needs roughly seven or eight circuits. A kitchen built in Mesa or Chandler in 1988 often has three. That gap is the electrical budget, and it is worth understanding before the demo starts rather than after.
The Short Answer
For a typical all-electric kitchen, the list looks like this:
Two 20 amp small appliance circuits
for the countertop receptacles. This is a minimum, not a target, and those circuits are not allowed to feed the lights or anything outside the countertop and dining areas.
One dedicated circuit for the refrigerator.

Technically there is some flexibility here, but in practice every kitchen we wire gets its own fridge circuit, because you do not want a tripped breaker on a weekend away to cost you everything in the freezer.
One circuit for the dishwasher
, which also needs ground fault protection.
One circuit for the garbage disposal.
A disposal and dishwasher can share in limited cases, but separating them is cleaner and matches most appliance manufacturer instructions.
One dedicated circuit for a built-in microwave
, whether it is over the range or in a cabinet.
One 240 volt circuit for the range or cooktop
, usually 40 or 50 amps. A separate wall oven gets its own.
One lighting circuit
for the ceiling cans, under-cabinet lighting, and any pendants.
Add a beverage fridge, a pot filler with a heated element nearby, a built-in coffee system, or a steam oven, and the count climbs from there.
What Older Valley Kitchens Actually Have

Go look in your panel. If your house went up in the 1970s or 1980s, the kitchen is commonly running on two small appliance circuits and a shared lighting circuit, and the microwave, the fridge, and sometimes the disposal are all riding on those same two.

That is why a lot of Valley homeowners live with the morning breaker dance: microwave plus toaster plus coffee maker equals a trip. People assume the breaker is weak. The breaker is fine. It is doing exactly what it is supposed to do on a circuit carrying three appliances that were never meant to share.
A remodel is the moment that gets fixed, because the walls are open and adding a circuit is a fraction of what it costs to fish one later.
Ground Fault and Arc Fault Protection
Two things have changed significantly over the last few code cycles and both will show up in your remodel.
GFCI protection has expanded a lot.

It used to be countertop receptacles only. Recent code has pushed it well past that, into the dishwasher circuit and, in newer cycles, essentially every receptacle in the kitchen including the 240 volt ones. What your specific city enforces depends on which code cycle they are on, which is one of several reasons this is not a great place to work from a YouTube video. If you want the basics of how the device itself works, we wrote up
how GFCI outlets work and how they are wired
Arc fault protection applies to most of the rest.
Arc fault breakers look for the signature of an arcing connection, which is the thing that actually starts electrical fires inside walls. In a remodel, new circuits generally get it.
The practical effect is that a modern kitchen panel has a lot more protective breakers in it than a 1985 panel did, and those breakers take space. Which leads to the part people do not expect.
The Panel Is Usually the Real Question
You cannot add five circuits to a panel that has no room and no capacity. On a lot of Valley remodels, the kitchen is the project and the panel is the actual cost.
Two separate issues:
Space.
Physical slots for breakers. Tandems can sometimes buy a little room, but plenty of panels are already full of them.
Capacity.

Whether the service itself can carry the new load. Going from a gas range to an induction cooktop, for instance, adds a serious 240 volt load that was not there before. So does adding a wall oven, and so does an EV charger somebody wants in the garage as part of the same project.
If the panel needs to come up, a like-for-like 200 amp replacement generally runs $5,200 to $6,500, or $6,400 to $8,750 when the meter base and panel are replaced together as an all-in-one. Our
guide to the signs you need a panel upgrade
covers what to look for, and the
panels page
has the details of the work.
Find this out in week one. The worst version of a kitchen remodel is the one where the cabinets are installed and then somebody discovers the induction cooktop has nowhere to land.
Outlet Placement, Islands, and the Details That Get Missed

Countertop receptacle spacing is governed so that no point along the counter is very far from a receptacle, which in practice means an outlet every few feet along any usable counter run, and any counter section a foot or wider gets one. It is a rule that exists so people stop running cords across sinks and cooktops.

Islands are the part that has genuinely moved across recent code cycles, and different Valley cities are on different cycles. The safe approach on an island is to plan for accessible power, get it designed with your electrician rather than assumed, and avoid the old trick of a receptacle mounted face up in the counter or tucked underneath where a cord can be pulled. Those have fallen out of favor for good reasons.
Other things that get missed constantly in remodels:
Under-cabinet lighting
needs a switched circuit and a plan for where the driver and wiring hide. Decide before the backsplash goes on.
Recessed lighting layout
is worth doing properly rather than putting cans on a grid. We covered the approach in our post on
recessed lighting installation in Phoenix
The range hood.

A big hood needs its own circuit and a real duct run, not a recirculating filter, if you actually cook. Ductwork is not our trade, and it is the one part of a kitchen where we hand people to our sister company
The Cooling Guy HVAC
(Arizona ROC 364481) rather than guess.
Appliance garages and drawer microwaves
need a receptacle located exactly where the cabinet maker expects it. Get the appliance specs before rough-in.
Going Gas to Induction

This comes up more every year, and it is straightforward as long as it is planned. An induction cooktop needs a dedicated 240 volt circuit, commonly 40 or 50 amps depending on the unit, run from the panel to the cooktop location.

The catch is that a gas kitchen was never wired for it. There is no existing 240 volt circuit behind that cabinet, so it is a new run plus a new breaker plus panel space, and it is exactly the sort of thing that is easy during demo and painful afterward. If induction is even on your list of maybes, run the circuit while the walls are open. An unused 240 volt circuit behind a cabinet is cheap insurance.
Timing: When the Electrician Should Be There
Kitchen remodels go well when the electrical happens in this order:
Before design is locked.
Panel evaluation and a load calculation. This tells you whether a panel upgrade is in the budget.
After appliances are selected, before rough-in.
Every circuit, receptacle location, and switch leg is decided off the actual appliance specs and the cabinet drawings.
Rough-in with the walls open.
New circuits, boxes, lighting, and any panel work.
Trim out.
Devices, fixtures, under-cabinet lighting, appliance connections, and testing.

The kitchens that get expensive are the ones where somebody tried to reuse existing circuits to save money and ended up with a brand new kitchen that still trips a breaker when the toaster and the air fryer run at the same time.
When to Call Us

Call us if you are planning a kitchen remodel and want to know what the electrical will require before you commit to a budget, if your current kitchen trips breakers when you run two appliances, if you are switching from gas to induction or adding a wall oven, if your contractor needs a licensed electrician for rough-in and trim, or if you just want somebody to open the panel and tell you honestly whether it can handle what you are planning.
We are happy to walk a kitchen before you are committed to anything. It is a lot easier to plan around a panel upgrade than to discover one mid-project.
At The Wire Guy Electric (Arizona ROC 365306), we handle
remodel wiring
and
dedicated circuits
as a family-owned electrical contractor, and we work alongside your cabinet and countertop trades rather than against their schedule.
We serve Mesa, Scottsdale, Gilbert, Chandler, Tempe, Queen Creek, Paradise Valley, and Fountain Hills.
